bib.title: Agent-FLAN: Designing Data and Methods of Effective Agent Tuning for Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Agent-FLAN: Designing Data and Methods of Effective Agent Tuning for Large Language Models. Zehui Chen, Kuikun Liu, Qiuchen Wang, Wenwei Zhang, Jiangning Liu, Dahua Lin, Kai Chen, Feng Zhao. Preprint (arXiv:2403.12881v1, 19 Mar 2024; the footer shows no venue). Year 2024.
COVERAGE: All 13 pages read, 47324 of 47324 chars. This includes the appendices (A experimental details, B dataset, C negative samples) and the references. Figures are not extracted as images; only their captions and in-text descriptions were read. Figures 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 carry numbers only as plots, so I report nothing from them except what the text states.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Agent-FLAN on Llama2-7B beats the re-implemented AgentTuning baseline on every column of the main table. The overall score is 41.7 against 38.2, and it beats AgentLM-7B (31.7) and FireAct-7B (16.6).
  number: Overall 41.7 vs 38.2 (AgentTuning*) vs 31.7 (AgentLM-7B) vs 27.2 (base Llama2-7B). The abstract says "by 3.5%", which matches 41.7 minus 38.2.
  setup: Llama2-7B. Held-in is trained on the AgentInstruct tasks plus ToolBench. Held-out is HotpotQA, SciWorld, WebArena and T-Eval. Agent-H is the hallucination score. * is the authors' re-implementation with the same amount of training data. Single run; no variance reported.
  quote: "Agent-FLAN (Ours) 2.01 28.5 20.0 4.68 66.0 89.1 41.7" and "AgentTuning* (Zeng et al., 2023) 1.89 25.4 16.8 2.71 61.8 84.5 38.2"
  where: Table 1, p.5
  Other rows, in the column order Held-in, HotpotQA, SciWorld, WebArena, T-Eval, Agent-H, Overall (the extraction does not show which column is Held-in versus Held-out; the Table 1 header is mangled):
  - GPT-4: 2.75, 52.1, 36.4, 6.28, 86.4, 94.2, 55.1
  - GPT-3.5: 1.59, 37.4, 21.2, 4.56, 84.0, 92.1, 47.8
  - Llama2-7B: 0.19, 22.6, 5.9, 1.2, 27.4, 78.7, 27.2
  - AgentLM-7B: 1.96, 22.3, 13.7, 0.74, 41.4, 80.6, 31.7
  - FireAct-7B: -, 26.2, 6.8, 0.25, 9.3, 40.4, 16.6

- claim: Agent-format training data (ReAct, JSON) is out-of-distribution relative to pretraining chat data. The loss on it falls fast while content loss stays high, so the model overfits the format and learns less reasoning.
  number: 0.54 vs 0.04 (loss on the formatted data vs normal data)
  setup: Training-loss curves on ToolBench ReAct data vs Flan2022 conversation data. The model is not stated for this figure. The "0.54 vs 0.04" is read from Fig 2. The explanation is the authors' speculation ("probably attributed").
  quote: "the loss associated with formatted data descends more rapidly to a low value, while keeping content loss still high (0.54 vs 0.04), indicating that the former leads to an inadequate learning process."
  where: Observation 1, p.3

- claim: Converting the ReAct and JSON agent data into multi-turn natural conversation (chat alignment) improves results over ReAct-format baseline training.
  number: +3.1 on T-Eval, +2.5 on HotpotQA (the text says "%" but these are points). Table 2: ReAct baseline 61.8 / 25.4; Align-Chat (All) 64.9 / 27.9.
  setup: Llama2-7B. Rows are T-Eval and HotpotQA. Single run. Note that Align-Chat (All) uses 37.3M tokens vs 19.2M for ReAct, so some of the gain may come from more tokens. "All (Weighted)" gets 66.3 / 28.5 with only 18.1M tokens.
  quote: "we can observe steady improvements by aligning training corpus into chat domain, i.e., 3.1% improvements on T-Eval, and 2.5% on HotpotQA."
  where: Sec 4.1 and Table 2, p.5

- claim: Loss is decomposed into four capabilities (instruction following, reasoning, retrieval, understanding). Instruction following and retrieval converge fastest. Reasoning and understanding are slower, and halving them hurts most.
  number: Halving reasoning or understanding gives -1.1 / -0.3 points (per the text). Table 2 T-Eval: All-Reasoning 63.8, All-Understand 64.6, All-Retrieval 65.3, All-Inst. 65.9, against 64.9 for All.
  setup: Llama2-7B. Ablation removes half of each capability's sub-mixture from an equal-weight mix. Evaluated on T-Eval and HotpotQA only. The differences are small and single-run.
  quote: "when reducing the portion of reasoning and understanding data to 50%, the final performance declines 1.1/0.3 points, respectively. By reducing the amount of retrieval and instruction following, the performance incurs little influence, and even improves."
  where: Sec 4.2, p.6; Table 2, p.5

- claim: Capability-weighted data balancing matches or beats the equal mix while using about half the tokens.
  number: 18.1M tokens, T-Eval 66.3, HotpotQA 28.5, vs All (equal mix) 37.3M tokens, 64.9, 27.9. Weights in the appendix: reasoning:retrieval:understanding = 1:0.25:0.75, plus 2000 instruction-following samples.
  setup: Llama2-7B. Weights come from the loss curves.
  quote: "The balancing weight for reasoning, retrieval, and understanding is set to 1:0.25:0.75. We additionally curate 2000 samples of instruction following data for training."
  where: Table 2, p.5; Appendix A, p.12

- claim: Negative-sample training (teaching when not to call tools) sharply reduces format and action hallucination. This is measured by the new Agent-H benchmark. T-Eval is unchanged.
  number: HReAct 9.9 vs 15.6 without NS (and 18.1 for AgentTuning); HGeneral 11.9 vs 13.5 (AgentTuning 14.0); HScore 89.1 vs 84.5 without NS (AgentTuning 83.9; base 78.7). T-Eval 66.0 vs 66.3 without NS.
  setup: Llama2-7B. Agent-H is built from glaive-function-calling-v2, with 1845 samples where the ground truth is a raw response and no tool call. A hallucination is counted when the response contains ReAct keywords ("Thought:", "Action:") or general ones ("I will use", "I need to call"). This is keyword matching on the surface format, not a semantic check. Lower H is better.
  quote: "Agent-FLAN 66.0 9.9 11.9 89.1" and "w/o NS 66.3 15.6 13.5 84.5"
  where: Table 3, p.7; Sec 4.3, p.6
  The negative samples are of two kinds: (1) no tools provided but the query asks for tools, and (2) tools provided but the query is normal conversation. Construction: 761 user queries from ToolBench, answered by gpt-3.5-turbo with no tools; for half of the queries, irrelevant tools are appended. Appendix C, p.12.

- claim: Existing mixed-data agent tuning (AgentTuning) raises agent scores but barely fixes hallucination.
  number: AgentTuning H_ReAct 18.1 vs base Llama2-7B 21.7; H_General 14.0 vs 21.0. T-Eval 61.8 vs 27.4.
  setup: Llama2-7B. Table 3.
  quote: "Despite the huge improvements in T-Eval score, the hallucination issue is quite severe gauged by Agent-H"
  where: Table 3 and Sec 4.3, p.6-7

- claim: Data scaling saturates early. 25% of the data gives most of the gain, and the authors conclude that diversity and quality matter more than volume.
  number: none in the text (the 25/50/75/100% results are plotted only, in Fig 7)
  setup: Llama2-7B, HotpotQA only.
  quote: "with only 25% training samples, the agent ability gains the most."
  where: Sec 5.1.1, p.7

- claim: Model scaling is steady with no saturation from 7B to 70B. The gain of Agent-FLAN over vanilla ReAct tuning persists as models get bigger.
  number: none in the text (Fig 8 only)
  setup: Llama2 7B, 13B and 70B, HotpotQA.
  quote: "as the model scale increases, the performance continuously improves without any saturation"
  where: Sec 5.1.2, p.7

- claim: Agent tuning does not hurt, and slightly helps, general ability.
  number: 7B: MMLU 49.7 (-0.3), GSM8K 22.1 (+0.2), HumanEval 15.5 (+0.4). 13B: 55.8 (+1.1) / 35.2 (+0.4) / 15.8 (+0.6). 70B: 68.5 (+0.5) / 64.6 (+0.1) / 32.9 (+0.8). The baselines are 50.0 / 21.9 / 15.1 (7B), 54.7 / 34.8 / 15.2 (13B) and 68.0 / 64.5 / 32.1 (70B), for general data only.
  setup: Llama2 family. Deltas are within a point, single run, no variance. The 7B MMLU score drops.
  quote: "Agent-FLAN 49.7 -0.3 22.1 +0.2 15.5 +0.4"
  where: Table 4, p.8

- claim: Training recipe and data size.
  number: 24,703 samples in total, of which ToolBench is 22,867. Mix is 1:1 ShareGPT to agent corpus, with 10% ReAct-format data and 90% conversation format. 1 epoch. LR 2e-5, warmup 4e-6, cosine schedule. GPUs 16 / 32 / 128 and batch size 32 / 32 / 128 for 7B / 13B / 70B.
  setup: Llama2. This is full SFT. No RL is used anywhere in the paper.
  quote: "we incorporate 10% data with ReAct format and the rest follows the format in Agent-FLAN. The models are fine-tuned on the training corpus with 1 epoch."
  where: Appendix A-B, p.12

LIMITS
- Authors concede: the train and eval sets cover only part of agent tasks. Only about 20,000 ToolBench samples were used, which is 10% of the whole dataset (quote: "we only choose roughly 20,000 valid samples from ToolBench, which is 10% of the whole dataset").
- Not shown: any comparison against RL or preference methods (SFT only). Nothing on multi-turn long-horizon use beyond the listed benchmarks. No seeds or confidence intervals. The gain over AgentTuning is only 3.5 points overall, against a re-implementation that the authors themselves built. Table 2 ablations use only T-Eval and HotpotQA.
- Confounds: the Align-Chat gain is not controlled for token count (37.3M vs 19.2M). The three-way ablation does not isolate the contribution of the chat-format change from that of the capability weighting.
- Agent-H is the authors' own benchmark, uses keyword matching, and is evaluated only on glaive function-calling data.
- The formula for HScore (Eq 1) as printed uses (1-HReAct) twice, a typo. The table values are consistent with the average of the two H terms (e.g. 0.5*((1-0.099)+(1-0.119)) = 0.89).
- Only Llama2 models were tested (2023 vintage; a dated base). The "3.5%" is in points, not relative.

BUILDS ON
- AgentTuning (Zeng et al., 2023): data, settings, 1:1 ShareGPT mix, and the baseline.
- The FLAN collection (Longpre et al., 2023), for the idea that mixture design matters, and for the "Flan2022" data used for the loss comparison.
- T-Eval (Chen et al., 2023c): the capability decomposition (instruction following, reasoning, retrieval, understanding) and a benchmark.
- ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023) and AgentInstruct. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022b) is the format being replaced.
- FireAct (Chen et al., 2023a) is a baseline. glaive-function-calling-v2 (GlaiveAI, 2023) is the Agent-H source. Also cites Chung et al., 2022 (Flan-PaLM scaling) for scaling analysis.

CODE: none (the paper says the code will be released at github.com/InternLM/Agent-FLAN). Example formats are in Figures 5, 10 and 11 (chat conversion; negative sample I with no tools, and II with irrelevant tools).

FIGURES (captions read; no images viewed)
- Fig 1, p.2: held-in and held-out comparison normalized to GPT-4. The visible per-task deltas are +1.8, +6.0, +8.8, +31.4, +4.0; the extraction does not say which task each belongs to.
- Fig 2, p.3: training loss on ReAct (ToolBench) vs conversation (Flan2022) data. This is the key evidence for the format-overfitting claim.
- Fig 3, p.3: loss per capability (retrieval, instruction following, reasoning, understanding); shows the different learning speeds.
- Fig 4, p.4: format hallucination vs action hallucination examples.
- Fig 5, p.5: conversion of a ReAct sample into multi-turn chat with elicit statements.
- Fig 6, p.6: four circumstances, from the user query and system prompt. (a) chat without tools, (b) tools present but irrelevant query, (c) tools needed but not provided, (d) agent task with tools.
- Fig 7 and 8, p.7: data and model scaling curves.
- Fig 9, p.8: qualitative ToolBench and Agent-H comparison.

PROBLEMS: The extraction had no instructions embedded in the text. The table header for Table 1 is garbled (the Held-In / Held-Out column labels run together), so which column is held-in is inferred. Figure-only numbers (Fig 1, 2, 3, 7, 8) are not extractable as text. Table 1's Held-In column values like 2.01 look like a different scale from the others, and the paper does not say what metric they are (possibly a normalized average across the held-in tasks); I did not guess.
